facts.fact: The Alonzo Church Papers at Princeton hold a correspondence folder "Rota, Gian-Carlo" and folders for Turing, Kemeny, Kleene and Rosser in the same subseries.
facts.evidence: "Rota, Gian-Carlo — 1 folder — dates not examined — Box 21, Folder 3" ; "Turing, Alan — 1 folder — dates not examined — Box 22, Folder 10" ; "Kemeny, John — Box 18, Folder 31" ; "Newman, M. H. A. (re. Alan Turing) — Box 20, Folder 6" (Series 2: Correspondence, Subseries 2A: Academic Correspondence). Collection title: "Alonzo Church Papers, 1924-1995".
facts.source: Finding Aid C0948, Princeton University Library, EAD fetched from (components C0948_c00409, c00440, c00342, c00385)

facts.fact: Courant asked the International Education Board to give von Neumann a fellowship to work with him at Göttingen.
facts.evidence: "…(John) von Neumann, be given a fellowship to come to Göttingen and work with him. At this time von Neumann did not yet have his Ph.D. Trowbridge replied that, although the degree was not a sine qua non for a fellowship, 'in this case I…'" ; "…Friedrichs, part of whose later work was to be strongly influenced by the work of von Neumann."
facts.source: Constance Reid, *Courant in Göttingen and New York* (Springer, 1976), p. 112 (index: "Neumann, John (Janos) von (1903–1957), 20, 111–12, 183, 198–99, 236, 278", p. 313). GB id IrGEAAAAIAAJ.

facts.fact: Hilbert proposed, and Courant then pressed, a fellowship to bring the 22-year-old von Neumann to Göttingen.
facts.evidence: "At the beginning of 1926 Hilbert proposed to the International Education Board that a 22-year-old Hungarian, Janos (John) von Neumann, be given a fellowship to come to Gottingen and work with him. At this time von Neumann did not yet have his Ph.D." … "While the ailing Hilbert was in Switzerland, Courant took up von Neumann's case." … [Courant to Trowbridge:] "Mr. von Neumann, in spite of his youth, is a completely exceptional personality ... who has already published a sufficient amount so that one can form a judgment of his technical ability."
facts.source: Constance Reid, *Courant in Göttingen and New York* (Springer, 1976), index gives von Neumann at pp. 20, 111–12, 188, 198–99, 236, 278.

facts.fact: Friedrichs, Courant's student and later NYU colleague, said his later work was strongly influenced by von Neumann's.
facts.evidence: "'We were wrong about that,' confessed Friedrichs, part of whose later work was to be strongly influenced by the work of von Neumann."
facts.source: Reid, *Courant*, ch. "1926–1928" (p. 111–112 by index). Same URL.

facts.fact: The Courant Papers hold pre-emigration correspondence with von Neumann.
facts.evidence: "Includes correspondence with John von Neumann, Otto Neurath (re: International Institute for the Unity of Science), Jakob Nielsen, Gottfried Noether, Herman Nohl…" — "Correspondence: Nagumo to Reichsverband, 1929-1933, Box: 7, Folder: 3"; and Folder 4: "Includes correspondence with Arnold Berliner … Otto Neugebauer, John von Neumann, Rolf Nevanlinna, Max H. A. Newman…"
facts.source: Guide to the Richard Courant Papers MC.150, same URL (Series I, Subseries A).

facts.fact: Von Neumann's work from the start of the war was on the equations of hydrodynamics and the theory of shocks.
facts.evidence: "In the middle 30's, Johnny was fascinated by the problem of hydrodynamical turbulence. It was then that he became aware of the mysteries underlying the subject of non-linear partial differential equations. His work, from the beginning of the Second World War, concerns a study of the equations of hydrodynamics and the theory of shocks."
facts.source: S. Ulam, "John von Neumann, 1903–1957," *Bull. AMS* 64 (1958), no. 3 part 2. Repo: 02_VON_NEUMANN/Ulam_von_Neumann_Obituary_BAMS_1958.md line 100.

facts.fact: Alonzo Church devised the λ-calculus, and the assumption identifying it with the computable functions came to be called Church's thesis; he was a principal founder of the Association for Symbolic Logic and its Journal.
facts.evidence: "one of the founders of the discipline of mathematical logic"; "one of the principal founders of the *Association for Symbolic Logic* and the *Journal of Symbolic Logic*"; "Church was the first to devise a formalism—the λ-calculus—within which it was possible to define a class of functions that coincide, arguably, with the intuitively computable functions."; "The list of his students, mathematical and philosophical, is striking as it contains the names of renowned logicians and philosophers."
facts.source: Oliver Marshall, "Alonzo Church," *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* (2021, rev. 2022), (quotations relayed by the page-fetch tool)

facts.fact: Fine Hall afternoon tea was where University and Institute people met; all the Institute people came.
facts.evidence: Tukey: "at the afternoon tea—which was where, you know, all the interesting interaction took place with people he asked me if I was at the University or at the Institute." … "graduate students had a lot of interaction, particularly in the early years, with a lot of people, because all the Institute people, including the junior people, turned up." … "While the Institute was in Fine Hall there was really very little distinction, except that the University faculty had to see to it that grad students, could pass prelims. The Institute people were not under the compulsion to teach, but a lot of them did."
facts.source: John Tukey (with A. W. Tucker), interviewed by Aspray, 11 April 1984, PMC 41

facts.fact: Church attended the Fine Hall teas.
facts.evidence: "afternoon tea in Fine Hall was really a continuation of Veblen's teas in Palmer Laboratory." … "Yes, I used to go to their teas in the afternoon."
facts.source: Church, PMC 5

facts.fact: Von Neumann took part in common-room mathematical discussion in Fine Hall.
facts.evidence: "Indeed I remember one occasion in the common room when there was some discussion going on of a topological theorem. Von Neumann immediately started out to construct his own proof of this."
facts.source: A. W. Tucker, interviewed by Aspray, PMC 34

facts.fact: Garrett Birkhoff was a frequent visitor to von Neumann at Princeton; continuous geometry grew out of that interest in lattice theory.
facts.evidence: "He was interested also in the lattice theory that Garret Birkhoff was developing at Harvard. Garrett Birkhoff, son of G.D. Birkhoff, was a frequent visitor to von Neumann at Princeton. It was out of the interest in lattice theory that von Neumann developed his so-called continuous geometry"
facts.source: Tucker, PMC 34

facts.fact: Church names Kemeny and Henkin together among his graduate students and says he thought well of Kemeny's dissertation.
facts.evidence: "Kemeny's dissertation concerned the relative strength of simple type theory and ZF set theory without replacement axiom. He wrote a dissertation which I thought well of"
facts.source: Church, PMC 5

facts.fact: Church and von Neumann consulted each other on set theory at Princeton.
facts.evidence: "Aspray: You did not have very much contact with him then? Church: Not too much. Occasionally there would be a question or a paper in set theory I would consult him about; and occasionally he would consult me."
facts.source: Church, PMC 5

facts.fact: Garrett Birkhoff personally described to Rota his first meeting with von Neumann.
facts.evidence: "Garrett once described to me his first meeting with von Neumann. After exchanging a few words they quickly got down to their common interest in lattice theory, and von Neumann asked Garrett, 'Do you know how many subspaces you get when you take all joins and meets of three subspaces of a vector space in general position?' Garrett immediately answered, 'Twenty-eight!', and their collaboration began at that moment."
facts.source: Many Lives, p. 1441

facts.fact: Rota, citing Ulam, on von Neumann rediscovering von Staudt's theorem while developing continuous geometries.
facts.evidence: "Von Staudt's theorem was so far removed from the mathematical mainstream that in the thirties von Neumann rediscovered it from scratch, giving much the same proof as von Staudt's while developing his theory of continuous geometries (I have been told by Stan Ulam that von Neumann, upon learning of von Staudt's work almost a century before, fell into a fit of depression)."
facts.source: IT (scan fragments; index: "von Staudt, 48, 147-148"; von Neumann, 146, 148)

facts.fact: Von Neumann's Princeton mathematics colloquium lecture on Gödel is what set Church and his students Kleene and Rosser to reading Gödel.
facts.evidence: Kleene: "It was von Neumann's math colloquium lecture on Gödel that put Church, Rosser, me and the rest of us onto reading Gödel." Also: "During Church's course itself we studied carefully Gödel's 1931 paper, which we got a preview of in a lecture by John von Neumann."
facts.source: S. C. Kleene and J. B. Rosser, interviewed by Aspray, 26 April 1984, PMC 23

facts.fact: Ulam dates the friendship at 25 years; Rota describes Ulam at the hospital.
facts.evidence: Ulam: "from a background of personal acquaintance and friendship extending over a period of 25 years." Rota: "Stan would visit him every day at Walter Reed Hospital in Washington, ready with a bagful of the latest jokes and prurient Los Alamos gossip. … After von Neumann died, Stan cried in the corridor outside the room, oblivious to anyone present."
facts.source: Ulam, BAMS 1958 (repo line 7); G.-C. Rota, *Indiscrete Thoughts* (1997), "The Lost Café" (repo: 04_ROTA/Indiscrete Thoughts.md line 313).

facts.fact: University and Institute mathematicians had offices in the same building, with no physical separation.
facts.evidence: "Between 1933 and 1939, when Fuld Hall was completed for the institute, Fine Hall also accommodated the institute's faculty and many visitors." … "Institute members were commonly employed as informal advisors of doctoral dissertations, and during this period, when both university and institute mathematicians had offices in Fine Hall, it was difficult to determine the official affiliation of visitors."
facts.source: William Aspray, "The Emergence of Princeton as a World Center for Mathematical Research, 1896–1939" (1988; repr. *A Century of Mathematics in America* II, AMS 1989),

facts.fact: Von Neumann came out to talk with Church's students about logic.
facts.evidence: Rosser: "Von Neumann actually wrote his Ph.D. thesis on definition of integers in logic. He would come out once in a while and have a chat with us about things." Kleene: "This was probably about '33-'34."
facts.source: PMC 23

facts.fact: Kleene credits von Neumann with bringing Gödel to the Institute.
facts.evidence: "Well, I'm sure von Neumann was back of it. … He heard Gödel present the preliminary version of his first incompleteness result and was very much excited by it. … So I'm sure he told the people at the Institute, 'You'd better get him over here.'"
facts.source: Kleene, PMC 23

facts.fact: The Institute for Advanced Study was housed in Princeton University's Fine Hall until Fuld Hall was completed.
facts.evidence: "While awaiting the construction of its first building, the IAS was originally housed in Princeton University's Fine Hall, until the completion of Fuld Hall in 1939. Einstein, one of the original IAS faculty, had an office in Fine Hall starting in 1933"
facts.source: Princeton University Archives (Mudd Library) blog, "Dear Mr. Mudd: Is the Institute for Advanced Study part of Princeton University?" (Oct. 2015),

facts.fact: The Church Papers hold a 1933 reprint and typescript of Church's "Postulates" paper with a note by Church to von Neumann, and three folders of von Neumann's writings.
facts.evidence: "'A Set of Postulates for the Foundation of Logic (Second Paper)' in Annals of Mathematics, vol. 34 1933 October pp. 839-864. 1 reprint, TMs(carbon), 46 pp., with ANS by Church to Prof. Von Neumann" (Box 1, Folder 9) ; "Burks, Arthur W., Goldstine, Herman H., and von Neumann, John" (Box 63, Folder 10) ; "Goldstine, H. H. and von Neumann, John" (Box 67, Folder 11) ; "Neumann, Johann v. (co-translator G. J. Massey)" (Box 74, Folder 3) (Series 5: Papers of Others).
facts.source: Finding Aid C0948, same URL (components C0948_c00011, c01050, c01107, c01227)

facts.fact: Einar Hille of Yale had been on the Princeton faculty until 1933, the years in which von Neumann arrived there (1930–31).
facts.evidence: "In 1923 Hille was promoted to assistant professor at Princeton, and in 1927 to associate professor. In 1933, he was appointed full professor at Yale University" ; KvN: "in 1930, for the first time, crossed the Atlantic, having accepted the invitation of Princeton University to become a guest lecturer for one year. In 1931 he became a member of the faculty of Princeton University"
facts.source: MacTutor, "Einar Hille,"; KvN Preface, p. xlvii

facts.fact: Von Neumann co-edited the *Annals of Mathematics* at Princeton from 1933 to 1957 and gave "lectures, too numerous to list" while at the Institute.
facts.evidence: "During his years as a professor at the Institute in Princeton, he gave lectures, too numerous to list, at various learned societies and academic in[stitutions]" ; "He served as a co-editor of the Annals of Mathematics in Princeton from 1933-1957"
facts.source: Ulam BAMS 1958 (repo lines 531–533)

facts.fact: Church and Turing obtained the definition of effective calculability and the unsolvability results almost simultaneously, in Church's own account.
facts.evidence: "the definitions of effective calculability and the results on the unsolvable decision problems are essentially the same. These were obtained by me and by Turing almost simultaneously. I think I was the earlier by six months or a year."
facts.source: Alonzo Church, interviewed by William Aspray, 17 May 1984, PMC 5

facts.fact: Courant wrote that he was with von Neumann "on absolutely friendly and open terms" at Princeton.
facts.evidence: "…Neumann on absolutely friendly and open terms. Likewise with Lefschetz. With others I have never talked about questions concerning German emigrés. But there is naturally in Princeton another group with whom I have much less contact."
facts.source: Reid, *Courant*, p. 183 (chapter headed "1935–1936"). GB id IrGEAAAAIAAJ.

facts.fact: Friedrichs recast his own work in von Neumann's Hilbert-space language.
facts.evidence: "…von Neumann's basic paper on Hilbert space, in which Hilbert's spectral theory becomes a special case in a general theory. That paper had been a revelation to him, and he had immediately translated his paper into von Neumann's Hilbert-space language. When he had returned to Germany after his visit to Courant in 1935, he had seen still another approach to the whole complex of problems, also involving Hilbert-space…"
facts.source: Reid, *Courant*, p. 198. GB.

facts.fact: Von Neumann to Birkhoff on the lattice of subspaces.
facts.evidence: "I would like to make a confession which may seem immoral: I do not believe absolutely in Hilbert space any more. … Now we begin to believe that it is not the vectors that matter, but the lattice of all linear (closed) subspaces."
facts.source: Von Neumann to G. Birkhoff, 13 Nov. 1935, in Rédei (ed.), *Selected Letters* (2005), p. 59 (repo corpus quotes.json)

facts.fact: Turing came to Princeton as a graduate student and wrote his dissertation there; Church discussed it with him.
facts.evidence: "He came to Princeton as a grad student and wrote his dissertation there. This was his paper about ordinal logics." … "I had a lot of contact with him. I discussed his dissertation with him rather carefully."
facts.source: Church, PMC 5

facts.fact: Garrett Birkhoff and von Neumann, "The Logic of Quantum Mechanics."
facts.evidence: "1936 With J. von Neumann. The logic of quantum mechanics. Ann. Math. 37:823–843." Also: "In the 1950s, in part inspired by his work as a consultant for the Westinghouse Electric Corporation and by conversations with von Neumann, Birkhoff changed research directions yet again"
facts.source: NAS Biographical Memoir of Garrett Birkhoff, (relayed by page-fetch tool)

facts.fact: Von Neumann wrote to Ulam from the Institute for Advanced Study from October 1936; the letters are in the Ulam Papers at the American Philosophical Society.
facts.evidence: "Dear Ulam, Letters to S. Ulam The Institute for Advanced Study School of Mathematics Fine Hall Princeton, New Jersey Oct. 3, 1936 many thanks for your kind letter…" ; "…Ulam papers, Archives of the American Philosophical Society, Philadelphia, language of original: English The Institute for Advanced Study School of Mathematics Fine Hall Princeton, New Jersey Oct. 4, [1937?] Dear Stan…" ; "…Ulam, November 9, 1943, written while staying at the Cosmos Club in Washington, D.C.…"
facts.source: M. Rédei (ed.), *John von Neumann: Selected Letters* (AMS/LMS, History of Mathematics 27, 2005), pp. 249, 251, 259. GB id AcAjDwAAQBAJ.

facts.fact: Irving Segal (Yale Ph.D. 1940, named by Rota among Yale's two pre-1950 stars) built his postulates for quantum mechanics as a modification of von Neumann's.
facts.evidence: "Segal submitted his thesis … to Yale in 1940" ; "During the winter of 1946-47 while at Princeton, Segal gave talks on his paper Postulates for general quantum mechanics. Here he presented a set of axioms which formed a modification of those put forward by von Neumann in 1932."
facts.source: MacTutor, "Irving Ezra Segal,"

facts.fact: Rota on the friendship: Ulam "the only close friend von Neumann had"; Ulam ridiculed continuous geometries, Hilbert space and rings of operators to cheer him.
facts.evidence: "Stan was the only close friend von Neumann had. Von Neumann latched on to Stan and managed to be close to him as often as possible. Stan was the more original mathematician of the two, though he accomplished far less in mathematics than von Neumann did; von Neumann had an incomparably stronger technique. From their free play of ideas came some of the great advances in applied mathematics: the Monte Carlo method, mathematical experiments on the computer, cellular automata, simulated growth patterns." "He began to make fun of von Neumann's accomplishments. He would mercilessly ridicule continuous geometries, Hilbert space and rings of operators. Like everyone who works with abstractions, von Neumann needed constant reassurance against deep-seated and recurring self-doubts."
facts.source: IT, "The Lost Café," pp. 71–72 (index: von Neumann, 70–73). Repo lines 308–310.

facts.fact: Rota on Ulam's appointment as von Neumann's assistant.
facts.evidence: "Through Lefschetz' influence, Ulam was invited in 1936 to visit the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. He was assigned to be John von Neumann's assistant."
facts.source: IT, "The Lost Café," p. 67 (index: von Neumann, 67). Repo line 285.

facts.fact: *Continuous Geometry* (Princeton University Press, 1960) reproduces von Neumann's Princeton lecture notes of the mid-1930s, prepared by L. Roy Wilcox and first distributed in multigraphed copies by the Institute for Advanced Study; the edition, foreword (dated Kingston, Ontario, 14 December 1959) and notes are Israel Halperin's, with Wallace Givens helping on Part I.
facts.evidence: "… and III were given during the academic year 1936–37. The notes were prepared, while the lectures were in progress, by L. Roy Wilcox, and multigraphed copies were distributed by the Institute for Advanced Study. The supply was soon exhausted, and the notes have not been reproduced until now. In the present edition many slips in typing have been corrected, in Part I with the help of Wallace Givens. I have inserted a few editorial remarks" ; "he finally decided that the Princeton lecture notes, at least, should be reproduced. This is now accomplished with the publication of the present book. Kingston, Ontario, Canada — Israel Halperin — December 14, 1959" ; title page: "CONTINUOUS GEOMETRY BY John von Neumann — FOREWORD BY ISRAEL HALPERIN — PRINCETON UNIVERSITY PRESS" ; contents: "Edition and comments on the text by Israel Halperin … 283"
facts.source: Halperin Foreword (scan fragments); publisher's page: "This book, based on von Neumann's lecture notes…"

facts.fact: The Birkhoff–von Neumann paper and the Halperin–von Neumann paper, as listed in von Neumann's bibliography.
facts.evidence: "65. *The logic of quantum mechanics.* With G. Birkhoff. Ann. of Math. vol. 37 (1936) pp. 823-843." ; "76. *On the transitivity of perspective mappings.* With I. Halperin. Ann. of Math. vol. 41 (1940) pp. 87-93."
facts.source: Ulam BAMS 1958, bibliography (repo lines 691, 714)

facts.fact: About seventy research mathematicians of the University and the Institute shared Fine Hall.
facts.evidence: "Veblen could state around 1937 that in Fine Hall there were altogether approximately seventy research mathematicians and an intense activity. This figure included the members and visitors of the University, too. There was no physical separation in Fine Hall between the two groups, which intermingled freely." Also: "There was also of course a weekly joint mathematical club."
facts.source: Armand Borel, "The School of Mathematics at the Institute for Advanced Study," in *A Century of Mathematics in America* III (AMS, 1989),

facts.fact: Halperin: von Neumann lectured at Princeton in 1937–38 on continuous geometries with a transition probability.
facts.evidence: "Continuous Geometries With A Transition Probability (MS written in 1936–37) and is important in applications to quantum mechanics. Von Neumann lectured on this topic at Princeton in 1937–38, but detailed lecture notes did not become available."
facts.source: Halperin Foreword (scan fragments)

facts.fact: Von Neumann wrote a formal letter of reference for Alan Turing's Procter Fellowship at Princeton.
facts.evidence: "a formal letter of reference dated June 1, 1937, supporting Turing's application for a Procter Fellowship at Princeton for the year 1937-38."
facts.source: Andrew Hodges, "Turing Sources: von Neumann."

facts.fact: Von Neumann wrote the formal letter of reference supporting Turing's Procter Fellowship at Princeton for 1937–38.
facts.evidence: "The first is von Neumann's formal letter of reference dated June 1, 1937, supporting Turing's application for a Procter Fellowship at Princeton for the year 1937-38. The application was successful."
facts.source: Andrew Hodges, "What von Neumann knew of Turing in 1937-39," (original: Princeton University)

facts.fact: Von Neumann wrote a letter of recommendation for Turing dated 1 June 1937.
facts.evidence: "…letters of recommendation sent to him. One of these was from the Wizard himself, who wrote: Sir, June 1, 1937 … Von Neumann would have been asked to write the letter, because his name carried such weight."
facts.source: Andrew Hodges, *Alan Turing: The Enigma* (1983), p. 131. GB id BlPZ3sHHWpMC.

facts.fact: Von Neumann offered Church's doctoral student Turing a post at the Institute.
facts.evidence: "Alan Turing could have stayed in America. He was offered a post-doctoral position by John von Neumann." Also: "In particular, Turing renewed contact with John von Neumann there. (They had met in Cambridge in 1935)."
facts.source: Andrew Hodges, The Alan Turing Internet Scrapbook,. Also J. A. N. Lee, IEEE Computer Society "Computer Pioneers: John Louis von Neumann," : "Von Neumann invited Turing to stay on at the institute as his assistant but he preferred to return to Cambridge"

facts.fact: The Courant Papers hold four folders "Strauss, Lewis" and five Atomic Energy Commission folders, a 1958 statement on the structure of the IMS and the AEC Center, Los Alamos folders and a 1961 Los Alamos consulting agreement.
facts.evidence: "Strauss, Lewis, 1938-1959, Box: 85, Folder: 6" (also Folders 7, 8) ; "Strauss, Lewis, 1947-1968, Box: 85, Folder: 9" ; "Atomic Energy Commission, 1946-1960, Box: 26, Folder: 6" ; "Atomic Energy Commission Access Permit Etc. General File, 1959-1971, Box: 26, Folder: 7" ; "Atomic Energy Commission--General File, 1956-1957, Box: 26, Folder: 9" ; "Statement Concerning Structure of IMS and AEC Computing and Applied Mathematics Center, 1958, Box: 84, Folder: 6" ; "Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory, 1952-1953, Box: 60, Folder: 12" ; "Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory, 1955, Box: 60, Folder: 13" ; "Consulting Agreements--Los Alamos, 1961, Box: 35, Folder: 19" ; "NONR Contract 285 (44)--Correspondence, Proposals, Misc. Salaries [Office of Naval Research], 1958-1961, Box: 70, Folder: 18". Scope note: "Courant and the IMS's World War II and post-war government consulting work is also well-represented in the collection, especially his work with the Atomic Energy Commission, the Office of Naval Research and IBM."
facts.source: Guide to the Richard Courant Papers MC.150, same URL.

facts.fact: Von Neumann offered Turing a research assistantship at the IAS; Turing wrote that the offer was $1500 a year and that he declined.
facts.evidence: "Von Neumann himself offered a research assistantship at the IAS. This might have meant a certain priority being given to von Neumann's research areas—at that time in the mathematics associated with quantum mechanics and other areas of theoretical physics…" (p. 144); "…Neumann would carry great weight. In professional terms, this was a big decision. But all Alan wrote of the opportunity to Philip Hall on 26 April was: 'Eventually a possibility of a job here turned up', and to Mrs Turing on 17 May … offer of a job here as von Neumann's assistant at $1500 a year but decided not to take it.' For he had cabled King's to check that the fellowship had been renewed, and since it had, the decision was clear." (p. 145)
facts.source: Hodges, *Alan Turing: The Enigma* (1983), pp. 144–145. GB id BlPZ3sHHWpMC.

facts.fact: Whitman on her childhood contact with her father during his war work.
facts.evidence: "…in contrast to the hectic encounters, marked by hurried arrivals and departures, I had grown used to. Once we reached Los Alamos, my father exuded boyish enthusiasm as he showed me around those areas I was allowed to enter—all the buildings where bomb-related work was conducted remained strictly off-limits" ; "the years 1940-43, while my father was deeply involved in military consulting and the development of the atomic bomb"
facts.source: Whitman, *The Martian's Daughter* (pp. 45–46). Same URL.

facts.fact: Whitman: her father was "deeply involved in military consulting and the development of the atomic bomb" in those years.
facts.evidence: "…military consulting and the development of the atomic bomb, culminated in the publication of the pathbreaking Theory of Games and Economic Behavior. Even in the midst of this enormous project, squeezed into spare moments snatched from…"
facts.source: Marina von Neumann Whitman, *The Martian's Daughter: A Memoir* (University of Michigan Press, 2012), p. 24. GB id lryyypm3mRAC.

facts.fact: Whitman: her encounters with her father were "marked by hurried arrivals and departures."
facts.evidence: "…hurried arrivals and departures, I had grown used to. Once we reached Los Alamos, my father exuded boyish enthusiasm as he showed me around those areas I was allowed to enter—all the buildings where bomb-related work was conducted…"
facts.source: Whitman, *The Martian's Daughter*, p. 45. GB.

facts.fact: Rota: Kakutani and Rickart joined Yale after the war; by the early fifties nearly every younger Yale mathematician worked in functional analysis; the core of graduate education was Dunford's course in linear operators.
facts.evidence: "After the end of World War II, Shizuo Kakutani came from Japan, and Charles Rickart from Michigan. By the early fifties, just about every younger mathematician at Yale was working in functional analysis, and the weekly seminars were attended by well over fifty people. The core of graduate education in mathematics was Dunford's course in linear operators. Everyone who was interested in mathematics at Yale eventually went through the experience, even such brilliant undergraduates as Andy Gleason, McGeorge Bundy and Murray Gell-Mann."
facts.source: IT, "Light Shadows," section "Mathematics at Yale," p. 29 (scan fragments; index: Kakutani, Shizuo, 29; Gleason, Andy, 29)

facts.fact: Kakutani spent 1940–42 at the Institute for Advanced Study on Weyl's invitation and took part in the group working with von Neumann on measure theory and ergodic theory.
facts.evidence: "Weyl invited Kakutani in 1940 to spend two years at the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton. Kakutani not only took great interest in the work of Weyl's group at Princeton but also the group of mathematicians working with von Neumann on measure theory and ergodic theory. He met many other young mathematicians at Princeton who would influence him such as Ambrose, Halmos, Doob, and Erdős. Kakutani also made many visits during which he met mathematicians such as Garrett Birkhoff, G D Birkhoff, Stone, Wiener, and Hille."
facts.source: MacTutor, "Shizuo Kakutani,"

facts.fact: Von Neumann spoke at Yale: he described plans for the IAS computer at the computer session of the Mathematical Association of America's summer meeting held at Yale University.
facts.evidence: "On 2 September, there was a session on computers at the summer meeting of the Mathematical Association of America held at Yale University. Von Neumann described plans for the IAS computer, and Howard Aiken described the Harvard Mark I and the Bell Labs relay calculator"
facts.source: Aspray (scan fragments; page c. 62–63 by running head "Logical Design 63")

facts.date: December, early 1940s (Reid: "That December"; year to be read off p. 236)
facts.fact: Courant, running an NYU seminar on stationary shocks, met von Neumann in Washington; von Neumann, working on moving shocks for explosion theory, arranged for his Navy co-worker Raymond Seeger to brief the NYU group on his results.
facts.evidence: "[Courant] ran a seminar at NYU on the theory of stationary shocks, important in aerodynamics. … That December he happened to run into John von Neumann in Washington. Von Neumann had been doing some work on moving shocks, important in explosion theory. Since he was about to leave for some new and secret project, he offered to have Raymond Seeger, a co-worker in the Navy's ordnance group for fundamental explosive research, brief the NYU people on his results."
facts.source: Reid, *Courant* (p. 236 by index).

facts.fact: Lax's Budapest mentors wrote to von Neumann asking him to look after the 15-year-old Lax; von Neumann interviewed him on arrival; in 1945 Courant intervened so the drafted Lax was sent to Los Alamos.

facts.fact: Rota: von Neumann "had already made up his mind to bring Stan with him" to Los Alamos.
facts.evidence: "Back in 1941 shortly after the United States entered the war, Stan (then still at Wisconsin) began to notice that von Neumann's letters were becoming infrequent. Curious about his friend's mysterious unavailibility, Stan managed one day to corner him in Chicago. He implored von Neumann to drag him out of his Wisconsin rut and to get him a job related to the war effort. The request fit perfectly with von Neumann's plans. He had already made up his mind to bring Stan with him to the newly founded Los Alamos laboratory, where the atomic bomb project was being launched. The choice of a set theorist for work in applied physics might seem eccentric, but in retrospect von Neumann made the right choice."
facts.source: G.-C. Rota, "The Lost Cafe", LAS 15, p. 29.

facts.fact: Rota on von Neumann bringing Ulam to Los Alamos.

facts.fact: Courant was a member of the OSRD Applied Mathematics Panel, which worked through contracts with institutions.

facts.fact: Before leaving for "some new and secret project" von Neumann had a Navy ordnance co-worker brief the NYU group on shocks; Reid dates NYU's shock-wave work from this.

This was the beginning of extensive work at NYU on shock waves, mainly by Friedrichs."
facts.source: Reid, *Courant*, p. 236. GB.

facts.fact: The IAS received an Applied Mathematics Panel contract on shock collisions following a conversation among von Neumann, Warren Weaver and Courant.

facts.fact: Waterman describes the Rota–Metropolis collaboration and Metropolis's computing career.
facts.evidence: "Other than Ulam his closest collaboration at Los Alamos was with Nick Metropolis, an elegant man who had a long association with the Lab. … In 1945, at von Neuman's invitation, Metropolis began to work with the ENIAC, and in 1947 he started a computer research group at Los Alamos that produced the remarkable series of MANIAC computers. … The MANIAC III, based on significance arithmetic, was built at the University of Chicago. For the last twenty years of his career, Metropolis worked in mathematics, much of it with Rota. One of their major contributions was in using concepts created for computers such as binary representation of numbers and "carry" operations and applying them to the foundations of real numbers. They brought forward a new idea, distinct from the usual Peano and Dedekind construction. There are four papers on those topics. They also studied the lattice of the faces of the n-cube, and they gave an explicit decomposition of the lattice into a minimal number of chains of lattice faces."
facts.source: Michael Waterman, in "Gian-Carlo Rota (1932–1999)", Notices of the AMS 47 no. 2 (Feb 2000), p. 205; offprint

facts.fact: Church gave Rota a task his own graduate students had declined: redo the work with Church's ternary connective "conditional disjunction."
facts.evidence: "Toward the end of the course I brought to him the sheaf of papers containing the solutions to the problems … He looked at them as if expecting them, and then pulled out of his drawer a note he had just published in *Portugaliae Mathematica*, where similar problems were posed for 'conditional disjunction,' a ternary connective he had introduced. Now that I was properly trained, he wanted me to repeat the work with conditional disjunction as the primitive connective. His graduate students had declined a similar request, no doubt because they considered it to be beneath them."
facts.source: *Indiscrete Thoughts* p. 6

facts.fact: Rota on what Church's course did.
facts.evidence: "The person lecturing to us was logic incarnate." … "Church's course permanently improved the rigor of our reasoning."
facts.source: *Indiscrete Thoughts* pp. 5–6

"Kemeny's seminar in the philosophy of science (which that year attracted as many as six students, a record) was refreshing training in basic reasoning." Kemeny to Rota: "Look at your teachers in Fine Hall, at how they treat one of the greatest living mathematicians, Alonzo Church."
facts.source: *Indiscrete Thoughts* p. 7

facts.fact: The AEC decided to place its UNIVAC in an eastern institution; Courant sought it for NYU.

He, Isaacson, and a member of the university administration represented NYU at the meeting in the Empire State Building."
facts.source: Reid, *Courant*, pp. 283–284. Same URL.

facts.source: Reid, *Courant*, p. 285. Same URL.

facts.fact: *Life* on the last paper and what he reasoned it meant.
facts.evidence: "After the last visitor had departed Von Neumann would retire to his second-floor study to work on the paper which he knew would be his last contribution to science. It was an attempt to formulate a concept shedding new light on the workings of the human brain. He believed that if such a concept could be stated with certainty, it would also be applicable to electronic computers and would permit man to make a major step forward in using these 'automata.' In principle, he reasoned, there was no reason why some day a machine might not be built which not only could perform most of the functions of the human brain but could actually reproduce itself, i.e., create more supermachines like it. He proposed to present this paper at Yale, where he had been invited to give the 1956 Silliman Lectures." Also: "He continued to preside over the ballistic missile committee, and to receive an unending stream of visitors from Los Alamos, Livermore, the Rand Corporation, Princeton."
facts.source: Blair, *Life*, 25 Feb. 1957. Same URL.

The little hospital bed would shake with the vibrations of von Neumann's big belly as he laughed himself to tears, the very tears that Stan was fighting to control. facts.fact: Ulam, on leave at MIT, visited the suite; a few days before the death he read Thucydides to von Neumann in Greek.
facts.evidence: "In the last months of his life, Johnny was hospitalized at Walter Reed Hospital. He occupied a very large suite reserved for high government officials. In the fall of 1956 we were living in Cambridge again, and I was a visiting professor at MIT on another leave from Los Alamos. I managed to travel to Washington and visit him a few times." "I will never forget the scene a few days before he died. I was reading to him in Greek from his worn copy of Thucydides a story he liked especially about the Athenians' attack on Melos, and also the speech of Pericles. He remembered enough to correct an occasional mistake or mispronunciation on my part. Johnny died in Walter Reed hospital, February 8, 1957. He was buried in Princeton in a brief Catholic service with a short eulogy by Admiral Strauss."
facts.source: Ulam, *Adventures of a Mathematician*, ch. "The Death of Two Pioneers," pp. 242–244.

facts.fact: Ulam's passage on Rota, pp. 263–265, with the sentences around "fill the gap left by the loss of von Neumann."
facts.evidence: "Sometime in the early 1960s I met Gian-Carlo Rota, a mathematician who is almost a quarter-century younger than I and definitely representative of the next generation. Or maybe even several generations later, for academically in mathematics [p. 263 / p. 264] … students where chronologically the difference is only a few years. Our relationship is not built on our age difference. Rota claims that he is greatly influenced by me. So I coined the expression 'influencer and influencee.' Rota is one of my best influencees. Banach, for example, I consider as an influencer. From the start I was impressed by Rota's feeling … analysis which is important in many of the large computational problems worked on the electronic computers. Rota's personality is compatible with mine. His general education, active interest in philosophy (he is an expert on the work of Edmund Husserl and Martin Heidegger), and, above all, his knowledge of classical Latin and ancient history, have made him fill the gap left by the loss of von Neumann. Indeed we often vie in quoting from Horace, Ovid, and other authors in a good-humored display of boasting erudition. Rota is also a true bon vivant, exceedingly fond of [p. 264 / p. 265] good wines and foods, especially those from Italy."
facts.source: Ulam, *Adventures*, ch. 13 "Government Science", pp. 263–265 (index: "Rota, Gian-Carlo, 72, 104, 129, 207, 263 ff, 268, 291"; "Husserl, Edmund, 264"). GB id g60wDwAAQBAJ and IA-FTS adventuresofmath0000ulam_v9h3 (fragments joined).

facts.fact: Ulam describes a Los Alamos computer experiment in recognition of handwritten letters and conjectures the brain works the same way.
facts.evidence: "I shall now describe a computer experiment Robert Schrandt and I did in the early sixties at Los Alamos. The experiment concerned the use of distances in the recognition of handwritten letters…" ; "The computer's decisions were correct in more than 80 percent of the cases!" ; "The conjecture is that in the brain, in the visual system and in the memory, perhaps only a few visual perceptions are permanently stored, and, when presented with another, the brain produces, for comparison, many deformations either of what is in the memory or of what is presented." ; "It is my speculation that in the brain, or more generally in the nervous system, there must be a mechanism that, perhaps in a qualitative way only, determines a distance between a perception stored in the memory and a newly presented perception." ; "However, I do not believe that now, or even in the near or distant future, it will be possible to gain what might be called a complete understanding of the brain's operation. My belief rests on very important and strange results in pure mathematics. These results, which date from 1930, are associated mainly with the name of Godel…"
facts.source: Ulam, "Reflections on the Brain's Attempts to Understand Itself", LAS 15, pp. 284–286.

facts.fact: In "The Barrier of Meaning" Rota reports Ulam's conversation on "the AI problem".

facts.fact: Rota on the Birkhoff–von Neumann paper: "indeed the long-awaited new 'logic.'"

facts.fact: Rota on continuous geometries and on von Neumann's search for a probabilistic setting for quantum mechanics.
facts.evidence: "Von Neumann worked hard at a probabilistic setting for quantum mechanics. His search for a quantum analog of a sample space led him to the discovery of continuous geometries. These geometries are similar to projective spaces, except that the dimension function takes all real values between zero and one. Von Neumann characterized continuous geometries as modular lattices and showed that noncommutative rings can be associated with continuous geometries which share properties of rings of random variables, in particular that there is the analog of a probability distribution. Sadly the applications of continuous geometries have hardly been explored; allow me to stick my neck out and mention one possible such application."
facts.source: Many Lives, p. 1444
